levels.title: Unique Stamps
levels.story: Odile wants every card in the catalogue to carry a stamp that no other card shares. Kit learns what makes a good stamp.

everyday.scene: Two members at the library are both called Sam Lee. The librarian asks for your member number instead of your name.
everyday.question: Why is a number better than a name?
everyday.answer: A name can be shared, but a number given to only one person leads to exactly one record. In a database, that kind of identifier is called a key.

lessons.title: The relational model
text: In the relational model, data is held in relations, which everyday speech calls tables. A row is a tuple and a column is an attribute. Each column has a domain: the set of values allowed in it, like whole numbers for a year.

text.text: Edgar Codd described this model in 1970. Most relational databases today use SQL, which Wikipedia calls an engineering approximation of it.

terms.meaning: A table, in the language of the model.
The set of values a column may hold.

lessons.title: Keys that pick out one row
text: A key is a column, or a group of columns, whose values pick out exactly one row. A column can only be a key if no two rows can ever share a value, and it is never empty. Any column that qualifies is a candidate key.
The designer picks one candidate as the primary key. PostgreSQL's manual says a primary key needs values that are both unique and not null, and a table can have at most one.

terms.meaning: Any column or group that could identify a row.

predict.prompt: In this members table, could name be a key? Why not?
predict.answer: No. Two members could share a name, and a key must never repeat.

lessons.title: Choosing well
text: A good key is unique, never empty and rarely changes. A suburb fails the first test, and a name does too. An email is unique, but people change it.
Many designers add a plain number the DBMS hands out, called a surrogate key. When no single column is unique, two or more can be combined into a composite key.

terms.meaning: A plain number added only to identify rows.
A key made of two or more columns together.

predict.prompt: A table records which member attended which workshop. Why can't member_id alone be the key?
predict.answer: A member can attend many workshops, so member_id would repeat. A pair, member and workshop together, can work.

activities.prompt: Which column makes the best primary key for the members table?

options.text: A member number the DBMS hands out

hints: Which choice can never be shared by two members?
Names, suburbs and birth years all repeat.
activities.explain: A plain number that is unique, never empty and never changes is the safest key.

activities.prompt: Sort each idea: would it make a good key or a poor one for a table of its own kind of thing?

items.text: A member number the DBMS hands out
A barcode printed on each book copy

hints: Ask: could two rows ever share this value?
Numbers made to be unique are good. Everyday facts repeat.
activities.explain: Keys must be unique. Surnames, genres, suburbs and birth dates repeat, so they fail.

activities.prompt: This members table has the columns member_id, name, email and suburb. Rows (member_id, name, email, suburb): (1, Sam, sam@a.example, Carlton); (2, Ana, ana@b.example, Carlton); (3, Sam, sam2@c.example, Fitzroy); (4, Ben, ben@d.example, Fitzroy); (5, Eli, eli@e.example, Carlton). How many columns could serve as a key, with no repeats and no gaps?
hints: Check each column for a repeated value.
Name repeats (Sam twice), and suburb repeats. Check the other two.
activities.explain: member_id and email are never repeated here, so both are candidate keys. The designer picks one as the primary key.

activities.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.

pairs.right: The set of values a column may hold
A key made of two or more columns

hints: Rows are tuples, columns are attributes.
A composite key needs more than one column.
activities.explain: The relational model's words map onto tables: relation, tuple, attribute, domain.

activities.prompt: Which rule must every primary key value follow?
hints: Think of what a key is for: picking out exactly one row.
A repeated or missing value cannot pick out one row.
activities.explain: A primary key must be unique and not null, so it always leads to exactly one row.

activities.prompt: A table records each member joining workshops, once per workshop. Members join many, and workshops have many members. What is the smallest key that works?
hints: A single column repeats here. What about two?
Each member and workshop pair appears only once.
activities.explain: Neither column is unique alone, but each pair appears only once, so the two together form a composite key.

feed.explain: A key picks out exactly one row.

feed.prompt: In the relational model, a row is called a...
feed.explain: Relation = table, tuple = row, attribute = column.

feed.prompt: Why do many designers add an id number instead of using an email as the key?

options.text: Emails can change, but an id never needs to
Emails are too long to store

feed.prompt: When do you need a composite key?
feed.answer: When no single column is unique, but two or more together are.

fieldNotes.title: Keys in everyday life
fieldNotes.text: A national identification number is a key in everyday life: a code that is unique to one person, so it can pick out exactly one record.

fieldNotes.title: A key also gets an index
fieldNotes.text: In PostgreSQL, declaring a primary key makes the DBMS build a lookup structure called an index, so duplicates are refused and rows can be found by key.

summary: You learned the words of the relational model, what makes a column a candidate key, and why a plain id often beats a name.
Odile stamps the first card with a number. "No two alike."

mistake.title: Using a name as a key
mistake.text: Names look unique until the day two people share one. A key must be unique for every row that could ever exist, so use a number made for the job.

levels.title: Matching Cards
levels.story: Cards in one drawer point at cards in another. Kit learns how those pointers are written, and how they are kept honest.

everyday.scene: A loan slip says "Member 3, Book 7". It does not copy the member's whole details and the book's whole details onto the slip.
everyday.question: How does the slip still lead you to both?
everyday.answer: It holds each one's id. A column of ids that point at another table's rows is called a foreign key.

lessons.title: A key that points
text: A foreign key is a column whose values are primary key values from another table. In loans, member_id says which row in members the loan belongs to. It is just a copy of the key, so nothing else needs repeating.
The table holding the primary key is the parent. The table holding the foreign key is the child.

terms.meaning: A column that points at another table's primary key.

lessons.title: Keeping pointers honest
text: A DBMS can enforce referential integrity: a foreign key value must match a primary key in the parent table. A loan for member 99 is rejected if there is no member 99. PostgreSQL's tutorial uses this very idea.
Deleting a member who still has loans is blocked by default too. A designer can choose another rule, such as deleting those loans along with the member.

predict.prompt: What should happen if you delete member 3 while loans still point at them?
predict.answer: By default the DBMS refuses. The designer can choose a rule, like removing their loans too.

lessons.title: Storing many-to-many
text: A one-to-many link needs one foreign key, placed on the many side: loans carry member_id. A many-to-many link fits in neither table, so it gets its own linking table.
Loans does this for members and books. Each row is one pairing, with a foreign key for each side, and it can also hold facts about the pairing, like the date.

terms.meaning: A table holding pairings for a many-to-many link.

activities.prompt: Sort each column: is it a primary key or a foreign key?
hints: A table's own id is its primary key.
A column that holds another table's id is a foreign key.
activities.explain: Each table's own id is a primary key. loans.member_id and loans.book_id point elsewhere, so they are foreign keys.

activities.prompt: Each member makes many loans. Where does the foreign key go?

options.text: A member_id column in the loans table
A loan_id column in the members table
Both tables, with all loans listed in each member's row

hints: The foreign key goes on the "many" side.
Many loans, one member each: loans point at members.
activities.explain: Each loan has one member, so loans carry member_id and point at members.

activities.prompt: Loans as (loan_id, member_id): (1, 1); (2, 1); (3, 2); (4, 3); (5, 3); (6, 3); (7, 5); (8, 1); (9, 3). How many loans belong to member 3?
hints: Look at the second number in each pair.
Count the pairs where the member is 3.
activities.explain: Loans 4, 5, 6 and 9 all point at member 3, so there are 4.

activities.prompt: Someone adds a loan for member 99, but members has no row 99. What does a DBMS enforcing referential integrity do?
hints: The foreign key must match a real primary key.
Nothing in members matches 99.
activities.explain: Referential integrity refuses a pointer to a row that does not exist.

activities.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.

pairs.right: The table whose primary key is pointed at
The table that holds the foreign key
A column pointing at another table's primary key
Holds the pairings of a many-to-many link

hints: Parents are pointed at. Children do the pointing.
A linking table has two foreign keys.
activities.explain: Children hold foreign keys that point at parents, and a linking table joins two parents.

activities.prompt: Students join many clubs, and clubs have many students. How should a database store the joins?

options.text: A third table with student_id and club_id as foreign keys
A list of club names inside each student's cell
A club_id column in students only

hints: A many-to-many link fits in neither table alone.
Each row of the third table is one pairing.
activities.explain: A linking table, one row per student and club pairing, is the standard answer.

feed.prompt: A foreign key is a column that...

options.text: Points at another table's primary key

feed.explain: It is a copy of a key from the parent table.

feed.prompt: A loan for a member who does not exist is...
feed.explain: A foreign key must match a real row.

feed.prompt: Why does a many-to-many link need its own table?

options.text: It fits in neither table without repeating or listing values
Tables can only hold two columns

feed.explain: One row per pairing keeps every cell a single value.

feed.prompt: Which side of a one-to-many link holds the foreign key?

fieldNotes.title: Linking tables behind authors and books
fieldNotes.text: Authors and books are many-to-many. In a relational database this is usually stored in a linking table (also called a junction or join table) that holds an author id and a book id.

fieldNotes.title: Pointers that cannot dangle
fieldNotes.text: Databases enforce referential integrity so a pointer never leads nowhere. Programs often check this themselves, but the DBMS can check it every single time.

summary: You saw that foreign keys point at primary keys, that a DBMS can refuse pointers to nowhere, and that many-to-many links get a table of their own.
Odile slides the drawers shut. "Every card now leads somewhere real."

mistake.title: Copying the whole record instead of its key
mistake.text: It is tempting to copy a member's name and address onto every loan. Then the same facts repeat and can drift apart. Copy only the key and let the pointer do the work.

levels.title: Tidy Shelves
levels.story: Odile's old index cards repeat the same address on dozens of cards. When someone moves, half the cards are missed. Kit sets out to tidy them.

everyday.scene: A club's attendance sheet has each member's phone number written next to every event they went to. One member changes number.
everyday.question: How many places must the secretary fix, and what if one is missed?
everyday.answer: Every row for that member. Miss one and the sheet disagrees with itself. Normalisation is the habit of keeping each fact in one place.

lessons.title: Facts that repeat
text: Suppose each loan row also stores the member's suburb. A fact now repeats on every loan, and that causes three kinds of trouble, called anomalies.

Update: change the suburb in some rows but not others, and the data disagrees. Insertion: a new member with no loans has nowhere to go. Deletion: remove someone's only loan and their details vanish too.

terms.meaning: The same fact stored in more than one place.
A problem caused by repeated facts.

predict.prompt: Ana moves to Brunswick, but only one of her three rows is fixed. What does the data now say?
predict.answer: That Ana lives in two suburbs at once.

lessons.title: The fix: split and link
text: Normalisation means rearranging tables so each fact is stored once. Spot a fact that depends on something other than the loan itself, move it to its own table keyed by what it depends on, and link the tables with a foreign key.
The suburb depends on the member, so it moves into members. Loans keep only member_id.

lessons.title: First, second and third
text: Designers name how tidy a table is with normal forms. First: every cell holds a single value, never a list.

text.text: Second: every non-key column depends on the whole key, which matters when the key has several columns. Third: non-key columns depend only on the key, not on each other.

text: Informally, a design is called normalised once it reaches third normal form.

terms.meaning: A named level of tidiness for a table design.

predict.prompt: A table has member_id, team and team_colour, and the colour depends on the team. Which form does that break?
predict.answer: Third. A non-key column (colour) depends on another non-key column (team).

text.text: Codd defined first normal form in 1970, and second and third in 1971.

activities.prompt: Sort each problem by the kind of anomaly it is.

items.text: Ana moves, but only 2 of her 3 loan rows are changed
A book title is spelt two ways in different rows
A new member who has not borrowed yet cannot be added
A new book cannot be listed until someone borrows it
Deleting a member's only loan also erases their suburb
Removing a book's last loan makes the library forget the book

hints: Update = changing a repeated fact. Insertion = adding something new. Deletion = removing something.
Ask what action causes the trouble.
activities.explain: Repeated facts make updates disagree, block new rows and lose data on deletion.

activities.prompt: One member has 40 loan rows, each with their suburb copied in. They move. How many rows must change?
hints: The suburb is copied into every one of their loans.
One row per loan, so as many as the loans.
activities.explain: All 40 rows must change, and missing one makes the data disagree.

activities.prompt: After the split, the suburb is stored only in the members table. When that member moves, how many rows must change?
hints: Where does the suburb live now?
It lives in exactly one row of members.
activities.explain: Just 1 row: their row in members. The loans do not store the suburb any more.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for tidying a table in order.
items: Find a fact repeated on many rows
Ask what that fact really depends on
Move it into its own table, keyed by that thing
Leave the key behind as a foreign key
Check each fact now lives in just one place
hints: You need to spot the problem before fixing it.
The key stays behind so the tables can still be joined.
activities.explain: Spot the repeat, find its owner, move it, link it, check it.

activities.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.

pairs.right: Every cell holds one value, never a list
Every non-key column depends on the whole key
Non-key columns depend on the key, not on each other
A problem caused by repeated facts

hints: First is the simplest. Third asks the most.
Anomalies are the trouble that normal forms prevent.
activities.explain: Each form rules out a kind of repeated fact.

activities.prompt: Which design keeps each member's suburb in just one place?

options.text: members(member_id, name, suburb) and loans(loan_id, member_id, book_id)
loans(loan_id, member_name, suburb, book_title) on its own
members(member_id, suburb) and loans(loan_id, member_id, suburb, book_id)
Two copies of loans, one per desk

hints: Count how many tables mention suburb.
Only one table should.
activities.explain: Suburb lives in members only, and loans point at members by id.

activities.prompt: A table has member_id, team and team_colour, and the colour depends on the team. Which normal form does this break?
hints: Is team_colour about the member, or about the team?
A non-key column depends on another non-key column.
activities.explain: Colour depends on team, not on the member key, which is exactly what third normal form forbids.

options.text: A repeated fact is changed in some rows but not others

feed.prompt: Where should a member's suburb be stored?
feed.explain: Each fact lives in one place.

feed.prompt: First normal form says every cell holds...

fieldNotes.title: Repeated facts drift apart
fieldNotes.text: Normalisation aims to reduce repeated data. When the same fact sits on many rows, copies can fall out of step: Wikipedia's example is an employee shown with different addresses on different records.

fieldNotes.title: Breaking the rules on purpose
fieldNotes.text: Some systems add repeated copies of data on purpose to make reads faster, because a query that joins many tables can be slow. This is called denormalisation, and it costs some write speed.

summary: You saw how repeated facts cause update, insertion and deletion trouble, and how splitting tables and linking them with keys removes it.
Odile files the last card. "One fact, one home."

mistake.title: Splitting without linking
mistake.text: Moving a fact into its own table is only half the fix. Keep a key behind as a foreign key, or the two tables can no longer be put back together.
